newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Petrochemical margins squeezed at both ends.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Petrochemical margins squeezed at both ends.

text.p: Petrochemical earnings reported by several major oil and chemical companies recently show margins getting squeezed at both ends, by firm crude oil prices and weak paraxylene prices.

Amoco Corp, Exxon Corp, Lyondell Petrochemical Co and others over the past few weeks have been posting third quarter earnings deflated by margins on paraxylene, which is used to make clothes and plastic containers. Analysts see the weak trend in this important product continuing into next year.
"A steep drop in paraxylene prices has cut into profits" this quarter, said industry analyst Bruce Lanni of Oppenheimer & Co.
"We don't see paraxylene prices turning around and we expect these price pressures to continue into 1996 and 1997," Lanni added.
Paraxylene prices have dropped from 41 cents a pound in the first quarter to a current 22 cents, and export prices have been slashed in half, data from Smith Barney shows.
Fourth quarter prices are to drop another two to three cents, analysts said.
"The industry is in an oversupply condition. There has been lower demand for a variety of products," said Lanni.
Paraxylene is used to make PET resin, the main material found in plastic containers. Paraxylene is also used to make polyester fibers found in many clothes.

But in addition to lower prices this year, the price of crude has gone up more than $5.00 per barrel since January, making the oil-derived feedstocks about five to 10 percent more expensive, said an analyst at Smith Barney.

Chemical companies are more exposed to rising crude oil prices than major oil companies, but even Amoco this quarter was down $170 million dollars before taxes on the previous quarter due to paraxylene's price slide, said Oppenheim chemicals analyst Jeffrey Spetalnick.
Amoco is the largest U.S. producer at 3.4 billion pounds per year. Exxon, which produces about 1 billion pounds annually, was $50 million down quarter-on-quarter.
"The biggest change has been in the price decline of paraxylene," said Spetalnick. "But it wasn't a big surprise, people just didn't expect it to stay where it was."
The forecast for the next quarter and beyond also looks poor. By 1998, U.S. capacity will have increased from a current 7.8 billion pounds to 9.9. billion due to expansions and new plants.
"Everyone will be producing 300 or 400 million pounds more, and so it will all add up," said the Smith Barney analyst.
Added Oppenheimer's Spetalnick: "Not only do we expect to see these paraxylene margins in the 4th quarter, but all through 1997, 98 and 99."
